title: 懸念強まる超長期国債　「物価高補正予算」4兆円に身構える海外勢
extracted_text:
国内債券市場でインフレや財政拡張への懸念が晴れない。とりわけ償還期間が10年を超える超長期国債の利回り上昇が目立つ。中東情勢の混迷が続くなか、防衛関連や経済対策に伴う財政悪化が改めて意識されている。

2022年度の岸田文雄政権（当時）が物価高対策で投じた4兆円が補正予算の目安とされ、その規模次第で振れ幅が大きくなりそうだ。

「（積極財政と金融緩和を組み合わせた）リフレ志向の政策を重視しつつ、中東混迷に伴う影響への対応を進めている点を踏まえると、日本の財政見通しを巡る懸念は強い」。米有力債券投資会社、ダブルライン・キャピタルでポートフォリオ・マネジャーを務めるビル・キャンベル氏はこうみる。同氏の見方を裏付けるかのように、足元では日本国債から距離を置く動きが広がる。

30日の債券市場では新発40年物国債利回りが前営業日比0.115%高い3.98%をつけた。節目の4%をつけていた3月末以来の高さで、1月につけた過去最高の4.2%台からも遠くない。新発30年債利回りも一時3.74%と同0.1%上昇した。超長期債は短中期債に比べて財政懸念をより織り込むとされる。

売りの根底にあるのが原油高騰に起因するインフレ圧力だ。エネルギー輸送の要衝であるホルムズ海峡の事実上の封鎖で、物価を巡る環境は様変わりした。広範な領域に物価高が波及し国民生活の重荷になるなか、ガソリン補助金などの経済対策が膨らむとの見方がもっぱらだ。

こうしたなか、プロが注目するのが30年債と2年債の利回り差（複利ベース）だ。市場における財政懸念の度合いを端的に示すとされ、3月以降に再び上昇している。30日には1月下旬以来およそ3カ月ぶりに2.3%台後半に上昇した。

3月以降は日銀が4月の金融政策決定会合で利上げに動くとの観測が高まっていた時期と重なる。ただ、それ以上に財政懸念を通じた超長期債への売り圧力が強まってきた証左が、この金利差拡大から読み取れる。

高市早苗首相は現時点で、中東情勢の緊迫化や原油価格高騰の対策を巡り「補正予算の編成が必要な状況とは考えていない」と明言している。ただ、市場では「ここまで原油価格が上がると、財政リスクを意識せざるを得ない」（国内証券の債券ディーラー）といった見方が散見される。

過去の実績で参考になりそうなのが、同じく原油高に伴う物価高対応に動いた22年度だ。

当時は22年度第1次補正予算では歳出の規模が約2.7兆円となった。大和証券の浜田浩史シニアエコノミストの試算によると、第2次補正予算の成立までに岸田政権が原油高・物価高対策に投じた金額は4.1兆円規模に上るという。今回も同等の水準が一つの参考になり得る。

ただ、当時は新型コロナウイルス禍への対応も重なっていたため、5兆円程度の予備費が活用できた。今回は1兆円程度と規模に違いがある。浜田氏は「災害対策なども考慮すれば、物価高対応で使える分はせいぜい5000億円程度ではないか」とみる。

ホルムズ海峡を巡る情勢が長引けば、その分こうした予算規模は膨らむことになる。仮に補正予算の検討が進む場合、5〜6月にかけてのヘッドライン（ニュースの見出し）に債券市場は振らされやすくなる。

海外勢はこれまで安定的に日本の超長期債に買いを入れてきた。ただ、高市政権の「責任ある積極財政」に対して懐疑的な声も聞かれ始めた。

シンガポールのヘッジファンド、モジュラーアセットマネジメントの最高投資責任者（CIO）、ジミー・リム氏は「原油ショックや金融正常化が迫るなか、積極的な財政支出はバランスの取れないものとなりかねない」と話す。「財政と金融の方針が乖離（かいり）すれば『債券自警団』が戻り、超長期ゾーンの落ち着きは失われかねない」

ダブルラインのキャンベル氏も、ガソリン補助金や消費税減税といった政策の組み合わせに加え、追加的な歳出を相殺できるだけの「信頼できる財源策が示されていない点が超長期債のタームプレミアム（上乗せ金利）の主因になっている」と指摘。長期や超長期ゾーンの日本国債はアンダーウエート（売り）姿勢を継続しているという。

発足時と比べて金融市場との対話姿勢を示すようになった高市政権。もっとも具体的な政策運営やその発信をひとたび誤れば、中東発でインフレの波が押し寄せるなか、市場のボラティリティー（変動率）が過度に高まり経済全体を揺さぶる恐れがある。

（生田弦己）

translated_text:
Concerns over inflation and fiscal expansion remain unresolved in the domestic bond market. Notably, the yield rise on ultra-long-term government bonds with maturities exceeding 10 years is conspicuous. Amid continuing Middle East turmoil, fiscal deterioration associated with defense-related and economic measures is being re-emphasized.

The Kishida administration in fiscal 2022 injected 4 trillion yen for inflation measures, which has become a benchmark for supplementary budgets, with the scale likely to cause significant swings depending on its size.

"Given that policy prioritizing reflationary measures combining active fiscal policy and monetary easing is emphasized, while efforts to address impacts from Middle East turmoil are ongoing, concerns over Japan's fiscal outlook are strong." So says Bill Campbell, Portfolio Manager at DoubleLine Capital, a major US bond investment firm. As if to substantiate his view, moves to distance from Japanese government bonds are spreading.

In the bond market on the 30th, the new 40-year government bond yield rose 0.115 percentage points from the previous business day to 3.98%. This is the highest level since late March when it hit the 4% threshold, and not far from the record 4.2% level hit in January. The new 30-year bond yield also rose 0.1 percentage points to 3.74% at one point. Ultra-long-term bonds are said to incorporate fiscal concerns more than short-to-medium-term bonds.

Underlying the selling is inflationary pressure stemming from surging crude oil prices. With the effective blockade of the Hormuz Strait, a key hub for energy transport, the price environment has changed dramatically. As inflation spreads across a wide range of areas and becomes a burden on people's lives, expectations that economic measures such as gasoline subsidies will expand are prevalent.

Amid this, what professionals are watching is the yield spread between 30-year and 2-year bonds (on a compound basis). It is considered a straightforward indicator of the degree of fiscal concerns in the market, and has been rising again since March. On the 30th, it rose to the high 2.3% range for the first time in about three months since late January.

Since March, this overlaps with the period when speculation that the Bank of Japan would raise interest rates at its April monetary policy meeting was high. However, more than that, evidence that selling pressure on ultra-long-term bonds through fiscal concerns has strengthened can be read from this widening yield spread.

Prime Minister Sanae Hichi said clearly that at the current time, she does not consider the situation to require compiling a supplementary budget regarding measures for the Middle East situation tensions and surging crude oil prices. However, in the market, views such as "once crude oil prices rise this much, we cannot help but be aware of fiscal risks" (from a domestic securities bond dealer) can be seen here and there.

What may serve as a reference from past performance is fiscal 2022, when measures were taken in response to inflation stemming from surging oil prices.

At that time, the first supplementary budget for fiscal 2022 had expenditure of about 2.7 trillion yen. According to calculations by Hamada Hiroshi, Senior Economist at Daiwa Securities, the amount the Kishida administration invested in oil price and inflation measures by the time the second supplementary budget was established reached about 4.1 trillion yen. This time, a similar level could serve as one reference.

However, at that time, responses to the COVID-19 pandemic were also overlapping, so reserve funds of about 5 trillion yen could be utilized. This time, the scale differs at about 1 trillion yen. Hamada notes, "Considering disaster response and other measures, the amount usable for inflation response would be at most about 500 billion yen, right?"

If the situation regarding the Hormuz Strait becomes prolonged, this budget scale will expand accordingly. If consideration of a supplementary budget progresses, the bond market will become prone to being shaken by headlines around May to June.

Overseas investors have stably bought Japanese ultra-long-term bonds until now. However, voices skeptical of the Hichida administration's "responsible active fiscal policy" have begun to be heard.

Jimmy Lim, Chief Investment Officer (CIO) at Modular Asset Management, a hedge fund in Singapore, says, "Active fiscal spending may become unbalanced amid oil shocks and financial normalization." "If fiscal and monetary policy directions diverge, the 'bond vigilantes' may return, and stability in the ultra-long-term zone may be lost."

Campbell from DoubleLine also points out that the lack of credible funding measures that could offset additional expenditure, combined with policies like gasoline subsidies and consumption tax cuts, is the main cause of the term premium on ultra-long-term bonds. The view is maintained that Japanese government bonds in the long and ultra-long zones are underweight (selling).

The Hichida administration, which has shown a stance of dialogue with financial markets compared to when it was established. However, should it once make a mistake in specific policy management or its communication, there is a risk that market volatility may excessively heighten and shake the entire economy as an inflationary wave from the Middle East crashes in.

(Narita Yuki)
title_en: Growing Concerns Over Ultra-Long-Term JGBs - Overseas Investors Brace for 4 Trillion Yen Inflation Supplementary Budget
